To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
phenols and phenolics are released into soils under Sahelian sorghum and that the amount of phenolics in soils depends on climatic conditions.
sorghum phenolic compounds are synthesized in the aerial parts of the plant, and are also present in the soil, where they can have allelopathic effects on the following crops.
sorghum phenolics are mainly released into the soil during the grain-filling stage.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification and quantification of phenolic compounds in sorghum and associated soil, in order to understand the allelopathic effects of sorghum on the following crops.
the synthesis of phenolic compounds in a grain sorghum (S. bicolor) genotype and their subsequent release into the soil.
the allelopathy of a sorghum genotype grown in Sahelian areas of Senegal, and the effects of its phenolic compounds released in soil on following crops.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the allelopathic effects of sorghum on subsequent crops in the Sahelian zone are due to the release into the soil of phenolic acids, which are synthesized in the vegetative parts of the sorghum plant.
phenolics are synthesized by sorghum plants in the Sahelian environment, that their amounts vary with years and sites and, consequently, that they can affect the following groundnut crops.
the phenolics released from the sorghum roots are the main allelopathic agents responsible for the negative effects of CE145–66 on groundnut crops.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the phenolic content of sorghum plants and associated soils is high, and that it is not affected by cropping or site factors, but by climatic ones.
phenolic content is higher in sorghum rows than in interrow soil samples, with the highest concentrations in rows in the year following sorghum harvest.
the allelopathic potential of sorghum is not only dependent on the genotype but is also strongly affected by the climatic conditions.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the phenolic content of sorghum is not affected by soil type, and is not affected by cropping conditions (e.g., soil fertility, water availability, or weed pressure).
sorghum is a source of phenols in the Sahelian soil, and that the phenolic compounds identified in the soil are the same as those found in the plant.
sorghum plants are able to release large amounts of allelopathy-related phenolic compounds into soil, and that these amounts are not significantly affected by the cropping system.
